analysis.one_liner: Lets bankruptcy trustees claw back executive bonuses, loans, and excess pay from failed companies.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee from September 2002 until the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Enron and WorldCom collapses, this bill would have changed bankruptcy law so that bonuses, loans, and other extraordinary pay paid to corporate insiders within a year before a bankruptcy filing could be pulled back into the company's bankruptcy estate. It also would have let trustees recover pay from executives who committed securities violations, fraud, or deceptive accounting going back four years. The money would go to the creditors owed by the failed company — which includes its employees and pension funds. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Creditors of companies that collapse amid executive misconduct — including employees owed wages and benefits, pension plans, investors, and suppliers. When executives collect big bonuses or loans shortly before a bankruptcy, that money currently often stays with them; this bill would have added it back to the pot that ordinary creditors share.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Creditors, employees, and pension funds of failed firms

how_it_helps.text: The bill would let a bankruptcy trustee claw back any transfer made to an insider, officer, or director in the year before filing for bonuses, loans, nonqualified deferred compensation, or other 'extraordinary or excessive compensation as determined by the court' [S3].

It would let trustees recover pay from officers, directors, and employees of publicly traded companies up to four years back when the executive committed a securities-law violation, fraud or manipulation in a fiduciary capacity, or illegal or deceptive accounting practices [S3].

The bill was written to build on the Public Company Accounting Reform and Investor Protection Act of 2002 (Sarbanes-Oxley), tying the longer clawback window to executives of covered public companies [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporate executives and insiders of companies that fail. Executives who took large bonuses, loans, or deferred pay shortly before a bankruptcy — or who committed securities fraud or accounting misconduct — would have to return that compensation to the bankruptcy estate. Companies and their insurers would also bear the cost of more clawback litigation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Executives and insiders of failed companies

drawbacks.text: The phrase 'extraordinary or excessive compensation as determined by the court' has no fixed definition, which invites litigation and inconsistent outcomes as judges decide pay package by pay package [S3].

The four-year clawback only triggers after an executive is found to have committed a securities violation, fraud, or deceptive accounting — a fact-intensive determination that could take years, complicating and delaying bankruptcy proceedings for everyone else involved [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the bill is a narrow tool: it applies only to companies in bankruptcy, so executives who enrich themselves and leave without triggering insolvency would face no clawback under this bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a targeted remedy for a real problem exposed by the Enron and WorldCom failures: executives extracting large payouts from companies on the way down, while employees and pension holders absorb the losses. Its main weakness is design, not aim — the vague 'excessive compensation' standard would have produced courtroom fights over what counts, and the fraud predicate for the longer lookback makes recovery slow. On balance it modestly shifted money from wrongdoers and overpaid insiders back to the creditors left holding the bag.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so the bill died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. Chuck Grassley introduced the bill on September 3, 2002, weeks after the Sarbanes-Oxley corporate accountability law was signed in July 2002 [S1].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].
No hearing, markup, or vote ever took place in the committee, and the bill never reached the Senate floor [S5].
One Senate Democrat cosponsored the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives and insiders of collapsing companies came out ahead: the rules in place when the bill died let them keep bonuses, loans, and deferred pay pulled out shortly before a bankruptcy, and the creditors — including employees and pension funds — recover nothing extra. Because the 107th Congress ended, the bill would have had to be reintroduced from scratch.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Executives who kept pay from failed firms

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred on September 3, 2002 — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and it died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, but no hearing or vote was ever held, so no party bloc ever took a recorded position on it.

industries.industry: Executives and directors of public companies
industries.note: The bill would have let bankruptcy courts pull their recent bonuses, loans, and deferred pay back into the estate — and reach back four years if they committed securities fraud or accounting misconduct. Their interest in the bill's failure ran against the employees and creditors left holding the losses.
New avoidance powers over executive pay would have generated additional trustee litigation and recovery work. That cost of pursuing clawbacks would be weighed against money returned to creditors.
